speaker_role: student/recent alum (MIT graduate, entrepreneurial background, sharing personal application experience; not an admissions officer)
commercial_incentive: none evident; recommends a free external essay (Paul Graham's) rather than any paid product
key_insights: His own admitted stats: SAT 780 Math / 750 Reading (1530 combined, self-described as slightly below MIT's average), 4.5 weighted GPA, top 7% class rank at a competitive high school; says he lacked major competition awards but still got in.

Advises against paying for summer programs, specifically calling Harvard's paid summer program 'almost like a scam' because admissions officers reportedly know it's pay-to-play and don't weight it heavily.
Credits a strong recommendation letter from an MIT-affiliated free summer program ('M semester,' where students take classes with MIT professors) as one of the biggest factors in his admission.

Central application strategy: build every extracurricular and essay around one consistent personal 'theme' or character (his was entrepreneurship/building real-world projects) rather than a scattered list of unrelated activities.

Heavily prepared for MIT's conversational-style alumni interview by researching the interviewer's LinkedIn/background beforehand; interview lasted roughly 2.5-3 hours, which he treats as a major application factor.
Argues a project doesn't need to be objectively groundbreaking to matter -- his own AI chatbot wrapper project was modest in substance but fit his overall narrative and grew a real user base.
Recommends reading Paul Graham's essay 'How to Do Great Work' as a way to find direction and passion when feeling lost about application strategy.
specific_numbers_or_facts: SAT 780 Math / 750 Reading (1530 combined); 4.5 weighted GPA, top 7% class rank
AP scores: Calc BC 5, CS Principles 5, World History 5, English Language & Composition 5, Physics C Mechanics 4, CS A 4
'ScholarAI' project reportedly grew to about 25,000 users and was 'closing in on five figures' of revenue
'Navaro' edtech project reportedly reached 700+ students and partnered with the local school system
notable_or_distinctive: Explicit 'build your application around one consistent theme' strategy framing, plus a pointed, named warning that paid pay-to-play summer programs (citing Harvard's) don't carry weight with admissions officers.
reliability_notes: Entirely self-reported personal anecdote with explicit survivorship-bias caveat ('if I applied another 100 times I don't think I could get in again'); the claim that Harvard's summer program is viewed as a 'scam' by admissions officers is the speaker's unverified opinion, not sourced to any admissions office.
